answer:
**Hypothesis (data-grounded answer to "What types of plant introductions were influenced by urban land use?"):**

Urban land use in the Barcelona province is associated primarily with **unintentionally introduced** non-native plants (accidental arrivals with contaminated seed, trade and tourism), secondarily with **gardening/horticultural introductions**, and **not** with agriculture–forestry introductions.

Concretely: (1) The probability of a plot containing Unintentional-pathway species rises steeply with the share of urban land in its surroundings — plots with unintentional aliens sit in landscapes ~5× more urbanized than plots without them (mean urban share 0.33 vs 0.07; point-biserial r = 0.48; adjusted logistic coefficient ≈ +2.4, p < 0.001 without the habitat factor, ≈ +2.1, p < 0.001 with habitat type only). Gardening introductions show a weaker positive association (mean urban share 0.28 vs 0.10; coefficient ≈ +1.1, p ≈ 0.03 without habitat; attenuated to non-significance, p ≈ 0.13, once habitat type is included). (2) AgriForest introductions show no positive urban association at any specification (unadjusted r = 0.04; coefficients ≈ 0 to −1.6, never significant), and at the coarsest/historical scales the trend is even negative — the agricultural–forestry pathway instead dominates the oldest introductions. (3) The two pathways linked to human-built environments also differ biologically: unintentional aliens have significantly broader invaded niches than gardening aliens (median niche breadth 0.84 vs 0.38, Kruskal–Wallis p = 0.047) and tend to occupy more plots, consistent with urban-associated ecological generalists. (4) The temporal record corroborates the mechanism: pathway composition changed radically over five centuries (χ² = 230, df = 6, p ≈ 10⁻⁴⁶), with Gardening rising from 17% of introductions before 1500 to 75% in 1985–2019 while AgriForest fell from 51% to 6% — the era of most intense urbanization coincides with dominance of ornamental/horticultural introductions and a persistent (~19–38%) accidental-introduction component, i.e. the two urban-coupled pathways.

**Important qualification (kept hypothetical, cross-sectional data):** the urban association of the Unintentional and Gardening pathways operates strongly through (or is partly absorbed by) the habitat type itself — urban-share is highly correlated with plots classified in the "Urban" habitat (r = 0.65), and in the fully adjusted model (urban share + 10 habitat types + environment + space simultaneously) all urban coefficients shrink to small, non-significant values with wide uncertainty. Thus the supportable statement is: *urban land use is associated with (and plausibly favours) unintentional and gardening introductions — unintentionally introduced generalists being the clearest signal — whereas agricultural–forestry introductions are independent of, and historically replaced by, these urban-linked pathways.* Causal attribution to urbanization remains a hypothesis, since the design is cross-sectional.

payload.hypothesis: Urban land use is associated primarily with unintentionally introduced non-native plants (accidental introductions with trade, contaminated seed and tourism) and, secondarily, with gardening/ornamental introductions; agriculture-forestry introductions show no positive association with urban land use and were historically replaced by the other two pathways. Unintentional aliens in urbanized landscapes are ecological generalists (broader invaded niche breadth), consistent with urban environments filtering for versatile, human-associated species. The association partly operates through the urban habitat type itself, and causal attribution to urbanization remains hypothetical (cross-sectional design).
payload.workflow: 1) Input QC: 632-plot tab-separated plot dataset (37 cols, zero missing), 81-species trait dataset, 12-cell temporal contingency table, 81-tip Newick tree (76/81 tip labels matched). 2) Main analysis (A): per-pathway hurdle models (logit presence + Poisson count on positives) on 632 plots with urban land-cover share (2009, 500 m buffer) as focal covariate; covariates: log elevation, 10-level habitat, log road/stream distance, annual temperature and rainfall, b-splines of UTM x/y; weak-ridge IRLS to handle complete separation in zero-positive habitat levels; joint bootstrap (1000) for pathway contrasts and CIs; sensitivity across 50/500/1000 m buffers x 1956/1993/2009; partial-adjustment models to diagnose habitat-mediated attenuation. 3) Auxiliary (B): Kruskal-Wallis comparisons of invasion-success metrics (invaded plots, occupancy, niche breadths, residence time, height) across pathways. 4) Temporal corroboration (C): pathway counts/shares per introduction period, chi-square test. Phylogenetic analysis skipped (no tree libraries available; 5 duplicate-species tip labels missing) - noted as limitation.
